people.label: Mark McCandlish
people.sub: Aerospace illustrator and conceptual artist; Disclosure Project witness, December 2000; relayer and draughtsman of the claimed Alien Reproduction Vehicle
people.narrative: Mark McCandlish is the origin point in print of a named craft, and he is not a witness to it. By his own account in the Disclosure Project's April 2001 Briefing Document he works principally as a conceptual artist for defence contractors, he missed the Norton Air Force Base air show of 12 November 1988 because of an illustration deadline, and everything he describes about a hangar holding three hovering saucer-shaped craft was told to him the following week by a friend who was there. He drew it, and the drawing is what propagates. The one contemporaneous document in the thread, an Aviation Week editor's unpublished 1990 interview notes, records the same direction of relay and records the witness disowning part of the drawing. He was declared deceased on 13 April 2021 at his home in Redding, California, of a gunshot wound to the head; the Shasta County coroner ruled suicide on an external examination that expressly declined an internal one. What makes him a node is proximity to the claim, not credibility: he held no office, no clearance is documented anywhere in the opened record, and his whole account is a relay of somebody else's sighting.
people.tierRationale: Node tier C carried from the dossier: proximity to the programme, not credibility. C/A/D were reasoned rather than transcribed, because the dossier proposed a node tier only. Custody proximity 0 and access 0 because no opened record gives him a clearance, an office or any contact with material; disclosure role 3 because his entire documented function is publication, which matches the board's existing treatment of steven-greer, the-black-vault and disclosure-project. Age is null: the coroner's '68 year old male' on 13 April 2021 and the arvp.co.uk '(1957 - 2021)' cannot both be right and no birth record was opened.

people.narrative: Everything substantive on this thread traces to one man, and the earliest document that carries him gives him a first name only. William B. Scott, then senior engineering editor of Aviation Week and Space Technology, interviewed 'Brad' for one paid hour in his Pasadena office on 3 December 1990 and compiled sixteen typed pages from two tapes. The profile there is of a mid-thirties Pasadena Art Center graduate with his own design business and clients including ski and motorcycle manufacturers, who claims a private pilot's licence but, in the interviewer's own note, 'didn't seem to have a lot of knowledge about military aircraft types'. He had refused to talk the previous summer, he told Scott he wished he had never seen the craft, and he disowned part of the drawing McCandlish had made from his description. The surname Sorensen reaches the record through McCandlish, not through this document, and no opened record carries it in the witness's own voice or over his own signature.

entities.label: Alien Reproduction Vehicle (ARV) / Flux Liner
entities.sub: Claimed saucer-shaped craft said to have been exhibited at Norton AFB on 12 November 1988; no record of its existence has been opened
entities.desc: The Alien Reproduction Vehicle, also called the Flux Liner, is a CLAIMED craft for whose existence no record has been opened, and the board carries it as a claim and not as an object: the entire account descends from one second-hand relay, in which a single man said he saw three such craft in a hangar and an illustrator who was not there drew what that man described. Everything on this node is therefore a description of a claim. Two primary documents carry that description, and they are why the node exists, not evidence that the craft does. The first is William B. Scott's unpublished 1990 interview notes, in which the witness gives the three craft nursery-rhyme names, guesses their diameters and expressly refuses to stand behind the figures, judges the build quality poor, and disowns part of the drawing made from his account. The second is the Disclosure Project's April 2001 Briefing Document, in which the illustrator gives the craft its two names in print and describes a capacitor stack, a central column carrying a secondary coil and a flywheel, forty-eight pie-slice capacitor sections, a Tesla-coil architecture running from two marine batteries at between half a million and a million volts, and a synthetic vision system in place of windows. The claimed lift mechanism is attributed to a Thomas Townsend Brown patent of the late 1950s or early 1960s; the board's own record of both Brown patents is that neither claims anti-gravity. Eric Davis, from inside the classification line, says no such craft exists. Every claimant on this thread runs into this node, which is the point of it.
entities.tierRationale: Node tier C: this is the thing claimed about, and nothing opened establishes it as an object. C/A/D were reasoned rather than transcribed, because the node is a session ruling rather than a dossier proposal: custody proximity 0 and access 0 because there is no opened record of custody of, or access to, any article; disclosure role 3 because the node's entire documented footprint is in the disclosure literature. dateStart is the claimed exhibit date, not an establishment date.

Just a guess; don't hold me to that.'

The 1990 interview notes give 'The small one was like 20 ft, the next 60 ft. diameter and the next one,...maybe 120 ft. diam. Just a guess; don't hold me to that.' The April 2001 Briefing Document gives the smallest as 'about 24 feet in diameter at its widest part, right at the base', the next as '60 feet in diameter at the base', and 'the largest of these vehicles was about 120 to 130 feet in diameter'. The arvp.co.uk FLUX 1988 page, read 18 September 2026, gives 'one with a 130-foot diameter, another with a 60-foot diameter, and a smaller one measuring 24 feet in diameter', with no disclaimer. Each retelling is more precise than the last about a figure the witness explicitly refused to stand behind.

Shown McCandlish's sketches in December 1990, Sorensen says of the manned vehicle: 'this is probably the farthest from what I saw, and no, I didn't see anything with an intake up above the windows like this', and 'mark extrapolates a bit too much'. claims.text: The account attributes the claimed lift effect to Thomas Townsend Brown. The 2001 testimony describes an experiment by 'Mark Stambough' that floated a plate capacitor at about a million volts 'in accordance with principles that had been described in a patent that was filed back in the late 1950s/early 1960s by a gentleman called Thomas Townsend Brown. Brown and another individual by the name of Dr. Biefield had done this, so this effect became known as the Biefield-Brown effect.' The direction of motion is given as toward the positively charged plate. The board's own record of both candidate patents is that NEITHER claims anti-gravity: US 3,187,206, filed 9 May 1958, opens 'This invention relates to an electrical device for producing thrust by the direct operation of electrical fields', and US 2,949,550, filed 3 July 1957, claims 'Thrust producing apparatus' operating by impressing high voltage between a body and an insulated electrode 'whereby to cause relative movement of an ionizable dielectric medium'. It is the ACCOUNT that reinterprets electrokinetic thrust as levitation.

entities.label: Norton AFB air show, 12 November 1988, and the alleged classified exhibit
entities.sub: Documented Air Force open house at which an SR-71A flew; the hangar exhibit alleged on the same date rests on one second-hand chain
entities.desc: One date carries two very different things. That an air show was held at Norton Air Force Base on 12 November 1988 is documented independently of the ARV account by a private photographic collection of Blackbird aircraft, whose captions place SR-71A 61-7962 at the base on that day. What is alleged to have happened inside a closed hangar on the same date rests on a single claimed eyewitness, and it is the load-bearing claim of the entire thread: three saucer-shaped craft of the same proportions in different sizes, a second unmanned diamond-shaped craft with 121 ports said to be cylindrical nuclear weapons, black cloth on metal rods dividing the space 'just like a car showroom', and a stated purpose of raising appropriations. The earliest document, taken about two years later, places the account only 'in early Nov. 88'; the exact date and the day of the week come from the 2001 testimony of the man who was not there. The same document records the witness saying he missed the introductions, saw no general officers, and did not know who was running the event.
entities.tierRationale: Node tier C carried from the dossier: the air show is documented and trivial, the exhibit is the load-bearing claim and rests on one witness at one remove. The node earns its place as the anchor both primary documents converge on. C/A/D were reasoned: custody proximity 1 and access 1 record a claimed display of claimed articles and a claimed invitation; disclosure role 2 because the alleged event is the subject of publication rather than its vehicle.
